📚 Today you learned

Reconciliation by Cash Delta — and Why a Second Snapshot Beats a First

When you can't see a trade confirmation directly, the account's cash balance is still a ledger — every fill moves it by a knowable amount. The first SPXC read (Sept 29) was built this way: cash moved from $330.60 to $432.16, a $101.56 jump that matches the $205 exit-limit on 0.5 shares (nets ~$101.50) far better than the $186.90 stop (~$92.45). That's an inference, not a confirmation — a single snapshot could in theory be a coincidence or a data error. What actually closes the case is today's second snapshot: Oct 6 shows the identical $432.16 cash figure, eight days later, with no new fills. One matching number could be luck; the same number showing up twice with nothing moving in between is a pattern. That's the real lesson — one data point is a clue, two independent ones that agree is close enough to proof that you can act on it, even before the formal confirmation.

Also today: Position Count Drift — the moment your tracking file and your broker disagree on how many positions you hold, every downstream number (cash, concentration %, risk score) is wrong in the same proportion, even the ones that look unrelated to the missing position.
